statement: Let $f$ and $g$ be real functions on a [finite set](c:finite-set) $S$ with $n$ elements. Assume that they vary together: $g(i) < g(j)$ implies $f(i) \le f(j)$ (for example, two [monotone sequences](c:monotone-sequence) with the same direction). Then $\left(\sum_{i \in S} f(i)\right)\left(\sum_{i \in S} g(i)\right) \le n \sum_{i \in S} f(i)\, g(i)$.

hypotheses.text: The index set $S$ is a [finite set](c:finite-set) with $n$ elements.
The functions vary together: $g(i) < g(j)$ implies $f(i) \le f(j)$ for all $i, j \in S$.

conclusion: $\left(\sum_{i \in S} f(i)\right)\left(\sum_{i \in S} g(i)\right) \le n \sum_{i \in S} f(i)\, g(i)$.

formal.difference: mathlib is more general: $f$ takes values in a linearly ordered semiring, $g$ in an ordered module over it, and the product is a scalar action. The real case is an instance.

proofs.name: Cyclic shifts and rearrangement
proofs.slogan: Expand the product of the two sums over the $n$ cyclic shifts of the index set, and bound each shifted sum by the rearrangement inequality.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. If $S$ is empty both sides are $0$; otherwise the proof lists $S$ as $s_0, \dots, s_{n-1}$ and shifts the indices cyclically.

roles.why: Finiteness gives a cyclic [permutation](c:permutation) of $S$ and makes every sum finite.
Varying together is the hypothesis of the rearrangement inequality.

steps.slogan: Fix a cyclic permutation $\sigma$ that moves $S$ around one cycle.
steps.detail: Write $S = \{s_0, \dots, s_{n-1}\}$ and let $\sigma(s_k) = s_{k+1 \bmod n}$. For $m = 0, \dots, n-1$ the map $\sigma^m$ is a [permutation](c:permutation) of $S$.

steps.slogan: Expand the product of the two sums over all shifts.
steps.detail: Since $\sigma$ is one $n$-cycle, every pair $(i, j) \in S \times S$ is $(i, \sigma^m i)$ for exactly one $i$ and one $m \in \{0, \dots, n-1\}$. Hence $\sum_i f(i) \cdot \sum_j g(j) = \sum_{m=0}^{n-1} \sum_i f(i)\, g(\sigma^m i)$.

steps.slogan: Bound each shifted sum by the unshifted sum.
steps.detail: The functions vary together, so the rearrangement inequality gives $\sum_i f(i)\, g(\tau i) \le \sum_i f(i)\, g(i)$ for every permutation $\tau$ of $S$. Take $\tau = \sigma^m$.

steps.slogan: Add the $n$ bounds to reach the stated inequality.
steps.detail: Each of the $n$ terms of the expansion is at most $\sum_i f(i)\, g(i)$. Hence $(\sum f)(\sum g) = \sum_m \sum_i f(i)\, g(\sigma^m i) \le n \sum_i f(i)\, g(i)$.

concepts.c:finite-set: The finite index set carries a cyclic permutation and finite sums.
concepts.c:monotone-sequence: Two monotone sequences with one direction are the main case of varying together.
concepts.c:permutation: Each shift of the index set is a permutation of it.

source.note: mathlib lists the finite set as one cycle (exists_cycleOn), expands with sum_smul_sum_eq_sum_perm, and bounds each term by MonovaryOn.sum_smul_comp_perm_le_sum_smul.

proofs.name: Sum over all pairs
proofs.slogan: Add the nonnegative products $(f(i) - f(j))(g(i) - g(j))$ over all ordered pairs and expand the sum.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; for $S$ empty both sides are $0$.

roles.why: A finite index set makes the double sum finite and lets it be expanded.
Varying together fixes the sign of each product $(f(i) - f(j))(g(i) - g(j))$.

steps.slogan: Show that each product $(f(i) - f(j))(g(i) - g(j))$ is nonnegative.
steps.detail: If $g(i) < g(j)$ then $f(i) \le f(j)$, so both factors are at most $0$ and the product is at least $0$. The case $g(i) > g(j)$ is the same with $i$ and $j$ exchanged, and $g(i) = g(j)$ gives $0$.

steps.slogan: Add the nonnegative products over all ordered pairs.
steps.detail: A sum of nonnegative numbers is nonnegative, so $\sum_{i, j \in S} (f(i) - f(j))(g(i) - g(j)) \ge 0$.

steps.slogan: Expand the double sum into four single sums.
steps.detail: The sum equals $\sum_{i,j} \big(f(i) g(i) - f(i) g(j) - f(j) g(i) + f(j) g(j)\big) = 2n \sum_i f(i) g(i) - 2 \left(\sum_i f(i)\right)\left(\sum_j g(j)\right)$.

steps.slogan: Compare the two forms of the sum and divide by $2$.
steps.detail: Steps 2 and 3 give $2n \sum_i f(i) g(i) - 2 (\sum f)(\sum g) \ge 0$. Dividing by $2$ gives the claim.

concepts.c:finite-set: Finiteness lets the double sum split into single sums.
concepts.c:monotone-sequence: Two monotone sequences with one direction are the main case of varying together.

source.note: The classical double-sum proof of Chebyshev's sum inequality; it uses only the sign of $(f(i) - f(j))(g(i) - g(j))$.

statement: Let $K$ be a [finite field](c:finite-field) of characteristic $p$. Let $f_1, \dots, f_m$ be [polynomials](c:polynomial-ring) in $n$ variables over $K$ with $\sum_i \deg f_i < n$, where $\deg$ is the [total degree](c:total-degree). Then $p$ divides the number of common zeros of $f_1, \dots, f_m$ in $K^n$.

hypotheses.text: The field $K$ is a [finite field](c:finite-field) of characteristic $p$, with $q$ elements.
The $f_1, \dots, f_m$ are [polynomials](c:polynomial-ring) in $n$ variables over $K$.
The [total degrees](c:total-degree) satisfy $\sum_{i=1}^m \deg f_i < n$.

conclusion: The number of common zeros of $f_1, \dots, f_m$ in $K^n$ is divisible by $p$.

formal.difference: mathlib indexes the polynomials by a finset and the variables by a finite type, and counts the zeros as a subtype of functions into $K$. The content is the same.

proofs.name: Indicator polynomial
proofs.slogan: Build a polynomial that equals $1$ on the common zeros and $0$ elsewhere, then show that its sum over $K^n$ is zero because its degree is too small.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, including $m = 0$ (then the number of zeros is $q^n$, divisible by $p$ since $n \ge 1$). The proof writes $q = |K|$, a power of $p$.

roles.why: In a [finite field](c:finite-field), $x^{q-1} = 1$ for $x \ne 0$, the unit group is cyclic, and $p \mid q$.
The polynomials define $F = \prod_i (1 - f_i^{q-1})$, whose [total degree](c:total-degree) is bounded.
The degree bound gives $\deg F < (q-1)n$, which makes every monomial miss some variable's top power.

steps.slogan: Form $F = \prod_i (1 - f_i^{q-1})$ and check that it is the indicator of the common zeros.
steps.detail: If every $f_i(a) = 0$, each factor is $1$ and $F(a) = 1$. If some $f_i(a) \ne 0$, then $f_i(a)^{q-1} = 1$ by Lagrange's theorem in the group $K^\times$, so that factor is $0$ and $F(a) = 0$.

steps.slogan: Turn the number of common zeros into a sum of values of $F$.
steps.detail: By step 1, $\sum_{a \in K^n} F(a) = N \cdot 1$ in $K$, where $N$ is the number of common zeros. Since $K$ has characteristic $p$, the number $p$ divides $N$ exactly when this sum is $0$.

steps.slogan: Bound the [total degree](c:total-degree) of $F$ by less than $(q-1)n$.
steps.detail: The factor $1 - f_i^{q-1}$ has degree at most $(q-1)\deg f_i$. So $\deg F \le (q-1)\sum_i \deg f_i < (q-1)n$ by the degree hypothesis.

steps.slogan: Show that $\sum_{x \in K} x^k = 0$ for $0 \le k < q - 1$.
steps.detail: For $k = 0$ the sum is $q \cdot 1 = 0$ because $p \mid q$. For $0 < k < q-1$ take a generator $g$ of the cyclic group $K^\times$. Then $g^k \ne 1$ and $S = \sum_x (gx)^k = g^k S$, so $S = 0$.

steps.slogan: Sum each monomial of $F$ over $K^n$ one variable at a time to get $0$.
steps.detail: A monomial $x_1^{k_1} \cdots x_n^{k_n}$ of $F$ has $\sum_j k_j < (q-1)n$ by step 3, so some $k_j < q-1$. The sum over $K^n$ is a product of one-variable sums, and the $j$-th one is $0$ by step 4. Hence $\sum_a F(a) = 0$.

steps.slogan: Combine the two facts to get $N \equiv 0$ modulo $p$.
steps.detail: Step 2 says $N \cdot 1 = \sum_a F(a)$ in $K$, and step 5 says this sum is $0$. So $N \cdot 1 = 0$ in $K$, which means $p \mid N$.

concepts.c:finite-field: The field supplies $x^{q-1} = 1$, a cyclic unit group and characteristic $p$.
concepts.c:polynomial-ring: The polynomials combine into the single polynomial $F$.
concepts.c:total-degree: The degree of $F$ must stay below $(q-1)n$ for the sum to vanish.

source.note: mathlib forms F = prod (1 - f_i^(q-1)), proves its values are the indicator, and applies MvPolynomial.sum_eval_eq_zero after bounding totalDegree.

statement: Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a [closed symmetric monoidal category](c:closed-symmetric-monoidal-category) with pullbacks and $d$ an object. Let $\mathrm{Chu}(\mathcal{C}, d)$ have objects $(A, X, r\colon A \otimes X \to d)$ and morphisms $(f, g)\colon (A, X, r) \to (B, Y, s)$ with $f\colon A \to B$, $g\colon Y \to X$ and $r(1 \otimes g) = s(f \otimes 1)$. Then it is a [star-autonomous category](c:star-autonomous-category).

hypotheses.text: The category $\mathcal{C}$ is a [closed symmetric monoidal category](c:closed-symmetric-monoidal-category) with pullbacks.
The object $d$ is any object of $\mathcal{C}$.

conclusion: The category $\mathrm{Chu}(\mathcal{C}, d)$ is a [star-autonomous category](c:star-autonomous-category).

proofs.name: Barr's outline
proofs.slogan: Build the tensor product and the internal hom from pullbacks, then check that swapping the two components is a duality with the dualizing object $(d, I)$.
proofs.scope: An outline of Barr's proof: the coherence checks for the tensor rest on pasting of pullbacks and are in the cited work. Pullbacks in $\mathcal{C}$ are needed for the tensor and the internal hom.

roles.why: The closed structure and the pullbacks of $\mathcal{C}$ build the tensor product and the internal hom; the symmetry gives the swap.
The object $d$ is the target of every pairing and gives the dualizing object $(d, I)$.

steps.slogan: Define the Chu category and check that it is a category.
steps.detail: Composition is $(f', g')(f, g) = (f'f, gg')$ and identities are $(1, 1)$. The two compatibility squares paste, so the composite is again a morphism. The first component is covariant and the second is contravariant, which gives the duality below.

steps.slogan: Build the tensor product of two objects from a pullback.
steps.detail: For $(A, X, r)$ and $(B, Y, s)$ take $A \otimes B$ as first component. The second component is the pullback $Z$ of $[A, Y] \to [A \otimes B, d] \leftarrow [B, X]$, with maps from $s$ and $r$ by adjunction. The unit is $(I, d, I \otimes d \cong d)$.

steps.slogan: Check that the tensor is functorial, associative and symmetric.
steps.detail: Both bracketings of a triple tensor have the same iterated pullback as second component, and the symmetry of $\mathcal{C}$ swaps the two legs of the pullback. Barr checks the coherence diagrams from the universal property of pullbacks.

steps.slogan: Construct the internal hom and prove the tensor-hom adjunction.
steps.detail: Set $[(A, X, r), (B, Y, s)] = (P, A \otimes Y, \cdot)$, with $P$ the pullback of $[A, B]$ and $[Y, X]$ over $[A \otimes Y, d]$. A morphism out of a tensor unwinds to a pair of maps that matches a morphism into the hom, by the adjunction in $\mathcal{C}$. So the Chu category is symmetric monoidal closed.

steps.slogan: Define the dual by swapping the two components and check that it is an involution.
steps.detail: Put $(A, X, r)^\perp = (X, A, r \circ \tau)$, where $\tau$ is the symmetry of $\mathcal{C}$. This is a contravariant functor, and $(A^\perp)^\perp = A$ exactly.

steps.slogan: Show that $\perp = (d, I)$ is a dualizing object.
steps.detail: The first component of $[(A, X, r), (d, I, \cdot)]$ is the pullback of $[A, d]$ and $[I, X] \cong X$ over $[A, d]$, which is $X$. So $[A, \perp] \cong A^\perp$ naturally, and $A \to [[A, \perp], \perp]$ is an isomorphism. This is the definition of a [star-autonomous category](c:star-autonomous-category), the structure behind multiplicative [linear logic](c:linear-logic).

concepts.c:closed-symmetric-monoidal-category: The base category supplies the tensor, the hom and the symmetry used throughout.
concepts.c:star-autonomous-category: The proof shows the Chu category has a dualizing object and an involution.
concepts.c:linear-logic: Star-autonomous categories interpret multiplicative linear logic.

source.ref: M. Barr, *-Autonomous categories, Lecture Notes in Mathematics 752, Springer, 1979 (appendix by Po-Hsiang Chu); M. Barr, The Chu construction, Theory and Applications of Categories 2 (1996), 17-35
source.note: Barr's appendix to LNM 752 defines the construction and proves it star-autonomous; the 1996 paper recasts the proof for a general closed monoidal category.

statement: Let $p$ be a [linear subspace](c:linear-subspace) of a [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$ over a division ring. Then $V$ has a subspace $q$ with $p \cap q = \{0\}$ and $p + q = V$.

hypotheses.text: The set $V$ is a [vector space](c:vector-space) over a division ring $K$.
The set $p$ is a [linear subspace](c:linear-subspace) of $V$.

conclusion: Some subspace $q$ of $V$ satisfies $p \cap q = \{0\}$ and $p + q = V$.

proofs.name: Retraction onto the subspace
proofs.slogan: Extend a basis of the subspace to a basis of the space, project onto the subspace along the new vectors, and take the kernel of that projection.
proofs.scope: All dimensions; the extension of a basis needs Zorn's lemma in infinite dimension. The cases $p = 0$ and $p = V$ give $q = V$ and $q = 0$.

roles.why: Every independent set of a vector space over a division ring extends to a basis.
A basis of $p$ is independent in $V$, and the retraction maps $V$ onto $p$.

steps.slogan: Extend a [basis](c:basis) of $p$ to a basis of $V$.
steps.detail: A basis $B_p$ of $p$ is linearly independent in $V$, so it lies in a maximal independent subset $B$ of $V$ (Zorn's lemma). By maximality $B$ spans $V$, since a vector outside the span could be added.

steps.slogan: Define a projection $\rho$ onto $p$ and set $q$ equal to its kernel.
steps.detail: Let $\rho$ be the linear map with $\rho(b) = b$ for $b \in B_p$ and $\rho(b) = 0$ for $b \in B \setminus B_p$. Then $\rho(v) = v$ for every $v \in p$. Put $q = \ker \rho$, a subspace of $V$.

steps.slogan: Show that $p$ and $q$ meet only in the zero vector.
steps.detail: Let $v \in p \cap q$. Then $\rho(v) = v$ because $v \in p$, and $\rho(v) = 0$ because $v \in q$. So $v = 0$.

steps.slogan: Split every vector into a part in $p$ and a part in $q$.
steps.detail: For $v \in V$ write $v = \rho(v) + (v - \rho(v))$. The first part is in $p$, and $\rho(v - \rho(v)) = \rho(v) - \rho(\rho(v)) = 0$, so the second part is in $q$.

steps.slogan: Combine the two facts to read $V$ as the [internal direct sum](c:internal-direct-sum) of $p$ and $q$.
steps.detail: Steps 3 and 4 give $p \cap q = \{0\}$ and $p + q = V$. So $q$ is a complement of $p$ and $V = p \oplus q$.

concepts.c:vector-space: The scalars form a division ring, which is enough for bases to exist.
concepts.c:linear-subspace: The subspace $p$ is the image of the projection and the one to complement.
concepts.c:basis: A basis of $p$ extended to $V$ defines the projection.
concepts.c:internal-direct-sum: The conclusion says that $V$ splits as $p \oplus q$.

source.note: mathlib takes q as the kernel of a left inverse of p.subtype (a basis extension) and applies LinearMap.isCompl_of_proj.

statement: Let $X_1, X_2, \dots$ be real [iid random variables](c:iid-random-variables) whose [moment generating function](c:moment-generating-function) is finite for every real $\lambda$. Put $\Lambda(\lambda) = \log E e^{\lambda X_1}$ and $S_n = X_1 + \dots + X_n$. Then $S_n / n$ satisfies a [large deviation principle](c:large-deviation-principle) with rate function $\Lambda^*(x) = \sup_\lambda (\lambda x - \Lambda(\lambda))$, the [Legendre transform](c:legendre-transform) of $\Lambda$.

hypotheses.text: The $X_i$ are real [iid random variables](c:iid-random-variables).
The [moment generating function](c:moment-generating-function) $E e^{\lambda X_1}$ is finite for every real $\lambda$.

conclusion: For every closed set $F$, $\limsup \frac{1}{n} \log P(S_n / n \in F) \le -\inf_F \Lambda^*$, and for every open set $G$, $\liminf \frac{1}{n} \log P(S_n / n \in G) \ge -\inf_G \Lambda^*$.

proofs.name: Chernoff bound and tilting
proofs.slogan: Get the upper bound from the exponential Markov inequality and the lower bound from a tilted law under which the target value is typical.
proofs.scope: Both bounds. The half-line bound is the core estimate; closed sets reduce to two half-lines, and the lower bound is proved on small intervals around each point, which suffices for open sets.

roles.why: Independence turns $E e^{\lambda S_n}$ into a power of one factor, and the law of large numbers holds for the tilted variables.
A finite $\Lambda$ is convex and differentiable, so the tilted law exists for every $\lambda$.

steps.slogan: Bound the probability of a half-line by the exponential Markov inequality.
steps.detail: Let $a \ge \mu = E X_1$ and $\lambda \ge 0$. Independence gives $P(S_n \ge na) \le e^{-\lambda n a} (E e^{\lambda X_1})^n$. By Jensen, $\Lambda(\lambda) \ge \lambda \mu$, so negative $\lambda$ never beat $0$, and the best bound is $e^{-n \Lambda^*(a)}$.

steps.slogan: Cover a closed set by two half-lines to get the upper bound.
steps.detail: If $F$ contains $\mu$, then $\inf_F \Lambda^* = 0$ and there is nothing to show. Otherwise $F \subseteq (-\infty, a] \cup [b, \infty)$ with $a < \mu < b$ and $a, b$ in $F$ or infinite. Step 1 and its mirror image bound the probability by $2 e^{-n \min(\Lambda^*(a), \Lambda^*(b))}$, and $\Lambda^*$ is convex with minimum $0$ at $\mu$, so this minimum is $\inf_F \Lambda^*$.

steps.slogan: Tilt the law of each $X_i$ so that the target value $x$ becomes the mean.
steps.detail: Let $\Lambda'(\lambda) = x$ and define the [change of measure](c:change-of-measure) $dP_\lambda = e^{\lambda X_1 - \Lambda(\lambda)}\, dP$ for each variable. Under $P_\lambda$ the $X_i$ are iid with mean $x$, so $P_\lambda(|S_n / n - x| < \delta) \to 1$ by the law of large numbers, and $\lambda x - \Lambda(\lambda) = \Lambda^*(x)$ because this concave function of $\lambda$ has derivative $0$ there.

steps.slogan: Undo the tilt to bound the probability of a small interval from below.
steps.detail: Write $P(|S_n / n - x| < \delta) = E_\lambda\big[e^{-\lambda S_n + n \Lambda(\lambda)}; |S_n / n - x| < \delta\big] \ge e^{-n(\lambda x + |\lambda| \delta - \Lambda(\lambda))} P_\lambda(|S_n / n - x| < \delta)$. Take $\frac{1}{n} \log$, let $n \to \infty$, then $\delta \to 0$. The liminf is at least $-\Lambda^*(x)$.

steps.slogan: Treat the values $x$ for which no tilting parameter exists.
steps.detail: The values $\Lambda'(\lambda)$ fill the open interval between the essential infimum and supremum of $X_1$. Beyond the closed interval, $\Lambda^*(x) = \infty$ and the bound is empty. At an endpoint $M$, $\Lambda^*(M) = -\log P(X_1 = M)$ and $P(|S_n / n - M| < \delta) \ge P(X_1 = M)^n$.

steps.slogan: Join the interval bounds to get the lower bound for open sets, and state the principle.
steps.detail: Let $G$ be open and $x \in G$ with $\Lambda^*(x) < \infty$, and choose $\delta$ with $(x - \delta, x + \delta) \subseteq G$. Steps 4 and 5 give $\liminf \frac{1}{n} \log P(S_n / n \in G) \ge -\Lambda^*(x)$; take the best $x \in G$. With step 2 this is the [large deviation principle](c:large-deviation-principle) with rate $\Lambda^*$.

concepts.c:moment-generating-function: Its finiteness makes $\Lambda$ smooth and convex, which the tilting needs.
concepts.c:large-deviation-principle: The two bounds proved here are exactly the principle with rate $\Lambda^*$.
concepts.c:legendre-transform: The rate function is the Legendre transform of $\Lambda$, attained at the tilt.
concepts.c:iid-random-variables: Independence gives the product formula, identical laws give one $\Lambda$.
concepts.c:change-of-measure: The tilted law makes the target value the typical value.

source.note: The Chernoff and tilting proof as in Dembo and Zeitouni, Large Deviations Techniques and Applications, theorem 2.2.3, which also drops the assumption that the moment generating function is finite everywhere.

statement: Every [permutation](c:permutation) of a [finite set](c:finite-set) is a product of [transpositions](c:transposition). The identity is the empty product.

hypotheses.text: The set $\Omega$ is a [finite set](c:finite-set).
The map $\sigma$ is a [permutation](c:permutation) of $\Omega$.

formal.difference: mathlib states the existence as a Trunc, a computable form of the existential statement, giving a list of swaps whose product is the permutation.

proofs.name: Peel off one moved point
proofs.slogan: Multiply the permutation by one transposition to fix a moved point, and repeat until only the identity remains.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, by induction on the number of points that $\sigma$ moves. The identity is the empty product, so sets with at most one point need no transposition.

roles.why: Finiteness makes the number of moved points a natural number, so induction applies.
Injectivity of $\sigma$ shows that the points fixed by $\sigma$ stay fixed after the multiplication.

steps.slogan: Count the points that the permutation moves.
steps.detail: Let $m(\sigma)$ be the number of $x \in \Omega$ with $\sigma(x) \ne x$. It is a natural number because $\Omega$ is finite, and $m(\sigma) = 0$ exactly when $\sigma$ is the identity.

steps.slogan: Treat the case that the permutation moves no point.
steps.detail: If $m(\sigma) = 0$, then $\sigma$ is the identity. The identity is the empty product of [transpositions](c:transposition).

steps.slogan: Multiply by one transposition to fix a moved point.
steps.detail: If $m(\sigma) > 0$, pick $x$ with $y = \sigma(x) \ne x$. Let $\sigma' = (x\ y)\,\sigma$. Then $\sigma'(x) = (x\ y)(y) = x$.

steps.slogan: Check that $\sigma'$ moves fewer points than $\sigma$.
steps.detail: Let $\sigma(z) = z$. Then $z \ne x$, and $z \ne y$ since $\sigma(y) = y = \sigma(x)$ would give $y = x$. So $(x\ y)$ fixes $z$ and $\sigma'(z) = z$; as $x$ is also fixed, $m(\sigma') < m(\sigma)$.

steps.slogan: Apply the induction hypothesis to $\sigma'$ and multiply back.
steps.detail: By induction $\sigma' = \tau_1 \cdots \tau_k$ with transpositions $\tau_j$. Since $(x\ y)$ is its own inverse, $\sigma = (x\ y)\,\sigma' = (x\ y)\,\tau_1 \cdots \tau_k$, a product of transpositions.

concepts.c:finite-set: Finiteness makes the count of moved points a natural number.
concepts.c:permutation: The map is injective, so the new product is again a permutation.
concepts.c:transposition: Each peeled factor is a transposition, and the product of them is the result.

source.note: mathlib's swapFactorsAux runs through a list of the points and multiplies by swap x (f x) whenever f x differs from x; the measure here is the same idea.

statement: In a finite simple [graph](c:graph) with vertex set $V$ and edge set $E$, the degrees satisfy $\sum_{v \in V} \deg(v) = 2\,|E|$.

hypotheses.text: The vertex set $V$ is a [finite set](c:finite-set).
The [graph](c:graph) is simple: it has no loops and no multiple edges.

proofs.name: Counting darts
proofs.slogan: Count the ordered pairs of adjacent vertices in two ways: by their first vertex, and by the edge that they form.
proofs.scope: Finite simple graphs. The empty graph gives $0 = 0$.

roles.why: Finiteness makes every count a natural number.
Without loops the two darts of an [edge](c:edge) differ, and without multiple edges an edge is a pair of vertices.

steps.slogan: Define the set $D$ of [darts](c:dart): ordered pairs $(u, v)$ with $u$ adjacent to $v$.
steps.detail: Each [edge](c:edge) $\{u, v\}$ gives the two darts $(u, v)$ and $(v, u)$. They differ because $u \ne v$, as the graph has no loops.

steps.slogan: Count the darts by their first vertex.
steps.detail: The darts that start at $v$ are $(v, w)$ for the neighbors $w$ of $v$, so there are $\deg(v)$ of them. Hence $|D| = \sum_v \deg(v)$.

steps.slogan: Count the darts by the edge that they carry.
steps.detail: The map $(u, v) \mapsto \{u, v\}$ from $D$ to $E$ is onto. Its fiber over $\{u, v\}$ is $\{(u, v), (v, u)\}$, which has two elements. Hence $|D| = 2|E|$.

steps.slogan: Equate the two counts of the set of darts.
steps.detail: Both counts equal the size of $D$, so $\sum_v \deg(v) = |D| = 2|E|$. This is double counting of the dart set.

concepts.c:graph: The theorem concerns a finite simple graph and its degrees.
concepts.c:finite-set: Finiteness makes every count a natural number.
concepts.c:edge: Each edge produces exactly two darts.
concepts.c:dart: The set of darts is the object counted twice.

source.note: mathlib counts darts: dart_card_eq_sum_degrees by first vertex and dart_card_eq_twice_card_edges by edge.

statement: The number $D_n$ of derangements of an $n$-element set, the [permutations](c:permutation) with no [fixed point](c:fixed-point), is $D_n = n! \sum_{k=0}^{n} \frac{(-1)^k}{k!}$.

hypotheses.text: The set $X$ is a [finite set](c:finite-set) with $n \ge 0$ elements.

formal.difference: mathlib shows that the count equals numDerangements, defined by $d_0 = 1$, $d_1 = 0$, $d_{n+2} = (n+1)(d_n + d_{n+1})$. The closed sum is the separate theorem numDerangements_sum, written with ascFactorial.

proofs.name: Recursion and its solution
proofs.slogan: Count derangements by the image of a fixed point to get $D_{n+2} = (n+1)(D_n + D_{n+1})$, then solve the recursion.
proofs.scope: All $n \ge 0$; $D_0 = 1$ (the empty permutation) and $D_1 = 0$ start the recursion, which is proved for sets of size $n + 2$.

roles.why: Finiteness makes $D_n$ a number that depends only on $n$ and lets the recursion split the set.

steps.slogan: Reduce the count to the standard set with $n$ elements.
steps.detail: A [bijection](c:bijection) between two $n$-element sets turns derangements into derangements by conjugation. So the number $D_n$ depends only on $n$.

steps.slogan: Split by the image of the first point and by whether the image returns.
steps.detail: Let $|X| = n + 2$ and fix $a \in X$. A derangement sends $a$ to one of $n + 1$ points $b$. If it sends $b$ back to $a$, the rest is a derangement of $n$ points; if not, skipping $a$ in the cycle gives a derangement of $n + 1$ points. Both are bijections, so $D_{n+2} = (n+1)(D_n + D_{n+1})$.
The recursion gives $D_{n+2} - (n+2) D_{n+1} = -(D_{n+1} - (n+1) D_n)$. So $D_{n+1} - (n+1) D_n$ changes sign at each step, and it equals $D_1 - D_0 = -1$ at $n = 0$.

steps.slogan: Divide by $n!$ and add up the differences.
steps.detail: For $n \ge 1$, step 3 gives $D_n / n! = D_{n-1} / (n-1)! + (-1)^n / n!$. Summing from $1$ to $n$ with $D_0 / 0! = 1$ gives $D_n / n! = \sum_{k=0}^n (-1)^k / k!$.

concepts.c:permutation: Derangements are the permutations that the recursion counts.
concepts.c:fixed-point: A derangement is a permutation without a fixed point.
concepts.c:finite-set: Finiteness makes the number of derangements a natural number.
concepts.c:bijection: A bijection of the sets carries derangements to derangements.

source.note: mathlib uses derangementsRecursionEquiv (card_derangements_fin_add_two) for the recursion, numDerangements_succ for the sign step and numDerangements_sum for the closed sum.

proofs.name: Inclusion-exclusion
proofs.slogan: Count the permutations that fix no point by inclusion-exclusion over the sets of points that are forced to be fixed.
proofs.scope: All $n \ge 0$; for $n = 0$ the sum has one term and $D_0 = 1$.

roles.why: Finiteness makes the sums over subsets finite and the counts $(n-k)!$ valid.

steps.slogan: Let $A_i$ be the set of permutations that fix the point $i$.
steps.detail: A derangement is a [permutation](c:permutation) outside $A_1 \cup \dots \cup A_n$. So $D_n = n! - |A_1 \cup \dots \cup A_n|$.

steps.slogan: Count the permutations that fix a given set $S$ of $k$ points.
steps.detail: A permutation in $\bigcap_{i \in S} A_i$ fixes the $k$ points of $S$ and permutes the other $n - k$ points freely. So $|\bigcap_{i \in S} A_i| = (n-k)!$.

steps.slogan: Apply inclusion-exclusion to the union of the sets $A_i$.
steps.detail: Inclusion-exclusion gives $D_n = \sum_{S \subseteq \{1, \dots, n\}} (-1)^{|S|} \left|\bigcap_{i \in S} A_i\right|$, where the empty $S$ gives the term $n!$.

steps.slogan: Group the subsets by size and simplify.
steps.detail: There are $\binom{n}{k}$ subsets of size $k$. So $D_n = \sum_k (-1)^k \binom{n}{k} (n-k)! = \sum_k (-1)^k\, n! / k!$.

concepts.c:permutation: Derangements are the permutations outside every set $A_i$.
concepts.c:fixed-point: The sets $A_i$ record the fixed points that are forbidden.
concepts.c:finite-set: Finiteness makes the subset sums finite.

source.note: The classical inclusion-exclusion count of derangements (Montmort's problem).

statement: Let $K$ be a [number field](c:number-field) with $r_1$ real and $r_2$ complex places. The [unit group](c:unit-group) of its [ring of integers](c:ring-of-integers) is the product of the finite cyclic group of roots of unity in $K$ and a free abelian group of rank $r_1 + r_2 - 1$.

hypotheses.text: The field $K$ is a [number field](c:number-field), a finite extension of $\mathbb{Q}$.

conclusion: $\mathcal{O}_K^\times \cong \mu(K) \times \mathbb{Z}^{r_1 + r_2 - 1}$, where $\mu(K)$ is the finite cyclic group of roots of unity in $K$.

formal.difference: mathlib gives a $\mathbb{Z}$-basis of the units modulo torsion, indexed by Fin (rank K), where the rank is the number of infinite places minus one. The product decomposition is exist_unique_eq_mul_prod, and finiteness of the torsion is a separate result.

proofs.name: Logarithmic lattice
proofs.slogan: Map the units to a space by logarithms, show that the kernel is the roots of unity, and that the image is a lattice of full rank.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. Write $r = r_1 + r_2 - 1$ and let $w_0$ be one infinite place; the proof follows mathlib's module on the Dirichlet unit theorem.

roles.why: Being a number field gives finitely many places, finitely many integers of bounded size, and Minkowski's theorem on the lattice of integers.

steps.slogan: Map each unit to the [logarithms](c:logarithm) of its absolute values at the places other than $w_0$.
steps.detail: Send a unit $u$ to $\ell(u) = (n_w \log |u|_w)_{w \ne w_0}$ in $\mathbb{R}^r$, where $n_w \in \{1, 2\}$. Then $\ell$ is a homomorphism. The product $\prod_w |u|_w^{n_w} = |N(u)| = 1$ shows that the omitted coordinate is minus the sum of the others.

steps.slogan: Show that the kernel of the map is the group of roots of unity.
steps.detail: If $\ell(u) = 0$, all conjugates of $u$ have absolute value $1$. Only finitely many algebraic integers of $K$ have all conjugates bounded, so $\ker \ell$ is a finite subgroup of $K^\times$, hence cyclic, made of roots of unity. Conversely a root of unity has all absolute values $1$.

steps.slogan: Show that the image of the map is a discrete subgroup.
steps.detail: A ball of radius $R$ in $\mathbb{R}^r$ contains only images of units whose conjugates are all bounded by $e^{cR}$. There are finitely many such integers, so the ball holds finitely many points of the image.

steps.slogan: For each place $w_1 \ne w_0$, construct a unit that is small at every other place.
steps.detail: Minkowski's convex body theorem gives a sequence $x_n$ of nonzero integers of norm at most $B$ whose sizes decrease at every place $w \ne w_1$. Only finitely many ideals have norm at most $B$, so by pigeonhole $x_m \mathcal{O}_K = x_n \mathcal{O}_K$ with $m < n$. Then $u = x_n / x_m$ is a unit with $|u|_w < 1$ for $w \ne w_1$.

steps.slogan: Show that these $r$ units give independent vectors in $\mathbb{R}^r$.
steps.detail: For the units $u_j$ built for the places $w_j \ne w_0$, the matrix of the $\ell(u_j)$ has negative entries off the diagonal. Each column sums to minus the $w_0$-coordinate of $\ell(u_j)$, which is positive. So each diagonal entry dominates its column, the determinant is nonzero, and the images span $\mathbb{R}^r$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the image is a [lattice](c:lattice-discrete-subgroup) of rank $r$ and split off the torsion.
steps.detail: A discrete subgroup of $\mathbb{R}^r$ that spans $\mathbb{R}^r$ is free abelian of rank $r$. The sequence $1 \to \mu(K) \to \mathcal{O}_K^\times \to \operatorname{im} \ell \to 1$ splits because the quotient is free. So $\mathcal{O}_K^\times \cong \mu(K) \times \mathbb{Z}^r$ with $r = r_1 + r_2 - 1$.

concepts.c:number-field: The field gives finitely many places and the lattice of integers.
concepts.c:unit-group: The unit group is the group whose structure the theorem gives.
concepts.c:ring-of-integers: The units are the invertible elements of the ring of integers.
concepts.c:logarithm: Logarithms turn the multiplicative group of units into an additive group.
concepts.c:lattice-discrete-subgroup: A discrete spanning subgroup of the space is a lattice with a basis.

statement: The partial sums $H_n = \sum_{k=1}^{n} 1/k$ of the harmonic [series](c:series) tend to $+\infty$: for every real $M$, some $N$ has $H_n > M$ for all $n \ge N$.

proofs.name: Cauchy condensation
proofs.slogan: Group the terms into blocks of length $2^k$, bound each block below by one half, and use that the partial sums increase.
proofs.scope: The whole statement. This is the condensation test for $f(n) = 1/n$, the route of the mathlib p-series test.

steps.slogan: Group the terms into blocks of length $2^k$.
steps.detail: For $k \ge 0$ let $B_k = \sum_{j=2^k+1}^{2^{k+1}} 1/j$. The block $B_k$ has $2^k$ terms.

steps.slogan: Bound each block from below by one half.
steps.detail: Every term of $B_k$ is at least $1/2^{k+1}$ because $1/j$ decreases. So $B_k \ge 2^k \cdot 2^{-(k+1)} = 1/2$.

steps.slogan: Add the blocks to bound $H_{2^m}$ from below.
steps.detail: The first $2^m$ terms are the term $1$ and the blocks $B_0, \dots, B_{m-1}$. So $H_{2^m} = 1 + B_0 + \dots + B_{m-1} \ge 1 + m/2$.

steps.slogan: Show that the partial sums are unbounded.
steps.detail: Given a real number $M$, choose an integer $m > 2M$. Then $H_{2^m} \ge 1 + m/2 > M$, so no bound holds for all partial sums.

steps.slogan: Pass from the powers of $2$ to all $n$ because the sequence increases.
steps.detail: The [sequence](c:monotone-sequence) $H_n$ is increasing, so $H_n \ge H_{2^m} > M$ for every $n \ge 2^m$. Hence $H_n \to \infty$, a divergent [series](c:series).

concepts.c:series: The partial sums of the series are the sequence that grows without bound.
concepts.c:monotone-sequence: Increase of the partial sums turns one large value into all later values.

source.note: mathlib shows not_summable_one_div_natCast through the p-series test summable_nat_pow_inv, which rests on Cauchy condensation (summable_condensed_iff_of_nonneg).

proofs.name: Integral comparison
proofs.slogan: Compare the sum with the integral of $1/x$, which grows like the logarithm.

steps.slogan: Bound each term below by an integral over one unit interval.
steps.detail: For $k \ge 1$ and $x \in [k, k+1]$ we have $1/x \le 1/k$. So $1/k \ge \int_k^{k+1} dx / x$.

steps.slogan: Add the bounds for $k = 1, \dots, n$ to get $H_n \ge \ln(n+1)$.
steps.detail: Summing the bounds of step 1 over $k = 1, \dots, n$ gives $H_n \ge \int_1^{n+1} dx / x = \ln(n+1)$.

steps.slogan: Use that the logarithm is unbounded to conclude.
steps.detail: Given $M$, take $N = \lceil e^M \rceil$. For $n \ge N$ we get $H_n \ge \ln(n+1) > M$. So $H_n \to \infty$ and the series diverges.

concepts.c:series: The partial sums of the series are the sequence that grows without bound.

source.note: The integral comparison $H_n \ge \ln(n+1)$, standard in calculus texts.

statement: Let $M$ be a set with two [binary operations](c:binary-operation) $\circ$ and $\star$ that have units $1_\circ$ and $1_\star$ and satisfy the [interchange law](c:interchange-law) $(a \star b) \circ (c \star d) = (a \circ c) \star (b \circ d)$. Then $\circ = \star$, the two units are equal, and the operation is associative and commutative: $M$ is a commutative [monoid](c:monoid).

hypotheses.text: The operation $\circ$ has a two-sided unit $1_\circ$ and the operation $\star$ has a two-sided unit $1_\star$.
The operations satisfy the [interchange law](c:interchange-law) $(a \star b) \circ (c \star d) = (a \circ c) \star (b \circ d)$.

conclusion: The two operations are equal, they have the same unit, and they make $M$ a commutative [monoid](c:monoid).

proofs.name: Insert units and interchange
proofs.slogan: Show that the two units agree, then write each product with units inserted and apply the interchange law to swap the operations and the order.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. Neither operation is assumed associative; associativity is derived in the fourth step.

roles.why: The units are inserted into products, and their equality is the first result.
The interchange law is the only rule that mixes the two operations.

steps.slogan: Show that the two units are equal.
steps.detail: Use $1_\star = 1_\star \star 1_\star = (1_\star \circ 1_\circ) \star (1_\circ \circ 1_\star) = (1_\star \star 1_\circ) \circ (1_\circ \star 1_\star) = 1_\circ \circ 1_\circ = 1_\circ$. Call the common unit $1$.

steps.slogan: Show that the two operations are equal.
steps.detail: For $a, b \in M$, the unit laws and the interchange law give $a \star b = (a \circ 1) \star (1 \circ b) = (a \star 1) \circ (1 \star b) = a \circ b$.

steps.slogan: Show that the operation is commutative.
steps.detail: Write $a \circ b = (1 \star a) \circ (b \star 1) = (1 \circ b) \star (a \circ 1) = b \star a = b \circ a$, where the last step uses the equality of the operations.

steps.slogan: Show that the operation is associative.
steps.detail: Write $(a \circ b) \circ c = (a \star b) \circ (1 \star c) = (a \circ 1) \star (b \circ c) = a \circ (b \circ c)$, using the equality of the operations for the first and the last step.

steps.slogan: Collect the results into a commutative [monoid](c:monoid).
steps.detail: The operation $\circ = \star$ is associative by step 4, has the unit $1$ by step 1, and is commutative by step 3. So $M$ is a commutative monoid.

concepts.c:binary-operation: The theorem concerns two operations on one set.
concepts.c:interchange-law: The law lets the proof swap the two operations in a product.
concepts.c:monoid: A monoid is an associative operation with a unit, which the proof delivers.

source.note: The argument of B. Eckmann and P. J. Hilton, Group-like structures in general categories I, Mathematische Annalen 145 (1962), 227-255.

statement: Let $A$, $K$ and $D$ be finite sets. Then some finite set $N$ has this property: every coloring $A^N \to K$ has a monochromatic [combinatorial subspace](c:combinatorial-subspace) of dimension $D$. Such a subspace fixes the coordinates outside disjoint nonempty blocks $S_e \subseteq N$ for $e \in D$, and sets all coordinates of $S_e$ to one letter $b_e \in A$.

hypotheses.text: The alphabet $A$ is a [finite set](c:finite-set).
The set $K$ of colors is finite.
The set $D$ that indexes the dimensions is finite.

conclusion: Some finite $N$ makes every $K$-coloring of $A^N$ constant on a combinatorial subspace of dimension $D$.

proofs.name: Reduction to Hales-Jewett
proofs.slogan: Apply the Hales-Jewett theorem to the larger alphabet $A^D$ and read each coordinate of a monochromatic line as $|D|$ coordinates over $A$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. No case split is needed: an empty $D$ gives a single point, which is monochromatic.

roles.why: A finite alphabet makes $B = A^D$ finite, so the Hales-Jewett theorem applies to $B$.
The Hales-Jewett theorem needs finitely many colors.
A finite $D$ keeps $B$ finite and makes $N = M \times D$ finite.

steps.slogan: Form the larger alphabet $B = A^D$ of functions $D \to A$.
steps.detail: The set $B$ is finite because $A$ and $D$ are finite. A letter of $B$ packs one letter of $A$ for each $e \in D$.

steps.slogan: Apply the Hales-Jewett theorem to the alphabet $B$ and the colors $K$.
steps.detail: The theorem gives a finite set $M$ such that every $K$-coloring of $B^M$ has a monochromatic [combinatorial line](c:combinatorial-line).

steps.slogan: Pull the given coloring back along the flattening map.
steps.detail: Let $N = M \times D$. A point $x \in B^M$ flattens to $\hat{x} \in A^N$ by $\hat{x}(i, e) = x(i)(e)$. Given $C\colon A^N \to K$, color $x$ by $C(\hat{x})$.

steps.slogan: Take a monochromatic line for the pulled-back coloring.
steps.detail: By step 2 there are a nonempty set $S \subseteq M$ and letters $c_i \in B$ for $i \notin S$ such that the point $x_b$, equal to $b$ on $S$ and to $c_i$ at $i \notin S$, has one color for all $b \in B$.

steps.slogan: Read the flattened line as a combinatorial subspace of dimension $D$.
steps.detail: For $e \in D$ let $S_e = S \times \{e\}$, a family of disjoint nonempty blocks. The point $\hat{x}_b$ sets the block $S_e$ to the letter $b(e)$ and fixes every other coordinate $(i, e)$ to $c_i(e)$. As $b$ runs over $A^D$, these points form the subspace, and all have one color.

concepts.c:finite-set: A finite alphabet keeps the enlarged alphabet finite.
concepts.c:combinatorial-subspace: The conclusion is a monochromatic subspace of dimension $D$.
concepts.c:combinatorial-line: A monochromatic line over the big alphabet becomes the subspace.

source.note: mathlib applies Line.exists_mono_in_high_dimension to the alphabet of functions from the dimension set to alpha and reindexes the line by the product of indices.

statement: An odd [prime number](c:prime-number) $p$ is a sum of two squares of integers if and only if $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$.

hypotheses.text: The number $p$ is an odd [prime number](c:prime-number).

conclusion: $p = x^2 + y^2$ for some integers $x, y$ exactly when $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$.

formal.difference: The declaration proves one direction only: a prime with $p \bmod 4 \ne 3$ is a sum of two squares, which includes $p = 2$. The converse, that no prime $3 \bmod 4$ is a sum of two squares, is not in it.

proofs.name: Gaussian integers
proofs.slogan: Factor $x^2 + 1$ over the Gaussian integers to show that $p$ is not prime there, then read the two squares from the norm of a proper factor.
proofs.scope: Both directions. The converse is a congruence check; the main direction uses the Gaussian integers $\mathbb{Z}[i]$.

roles.why: Oddness gives $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ from a sum of squares, and primality gives Wilson's theorem and the norm $N(\alpha) = p$.

steps.slogan: Show that an odd sum of two squares is $1$ modulo $4$.
steps.detail: A square is $0$ or $1$ modulo $4$. If $p = x^2 + y^2$ is odd, exactly one of $x, y$ is odd, so $p \equiv 0 + 1 = 1 \pmod 4$.

steps.slogan: Find $x$ with $x^2 \equiv -1 \pmod p$ when $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$.
steps.detail: Let $x = ((p-1)/2)!$. Pairing $j$ with $p - j$ in $(p-1)! \equiv -1$ (Wilson) gives $-1 \equiv (-1)^{(p-1)/2} x^2$. The exponent $(p-1)/2$ is even, so $x^2 \equiv -1$.

steps.slogan: Show that $p$ is not prime in the [Gaussian integers](c:gaussian-integer).
steps.detail: In $\mathbb{Z}[i]$, $p$ divides $x^2 + 1 = (x + i)(x - i)$. It divides neither factor, because the quotient $(x \pm i)/p$ has imaginary part $\pm 1/p \notin \mathbb{Z}$. So $p$ is not a prime element.

steps.slogan: Use unique factorization to show that $p$ is a product of two non-units.
steps.detail: The ring $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ is a [Euclidean domain](c:euclidean-domain) for the norm $N(a + bi) = a^2 + b^2$. So it is a [unique factorization domain](c:unique-factorization-domain), and irreducible elements are prime. As $p$ is not prime and not a unit, $p = \alpha\beta$ with neither factor a unit.

steps.slogan: Take norms of the factorization to find the two squares.
steps.detail: $p^2 = N(p) = N(\alpha) N(\beta)$, and $N(\alpha), N(\beta) > 1$ because non-units have norm greater than $1$. As $p$ is prime, $N(\alpha) = p$. Writing $\alpha = a + bi$ gives $p = a^2 + b^2$.

steps.slogan: Join the two directions into the equivalence.
steps.detail: Step 1 gives $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ from a sum of two squares. Steps 2 to 5 give a sum of two squares from $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$. Together they prove the equivalence.

concepts.c:prime-number: Primality gives Wilson's theorem and forces the norm of a factor to be $p$.
concepts.c:gaussian-integer: Factoring $x^2 + 1$ in the Gaussian integers detects the sum of two squares.
concepts.c:euclidean-domain: The norm gives division with remainder in the Gaussian integers.
concepts.c:unique-factorization-domain: Unique factorization makes irreducible elements prime.

source.note: mathlib shows p is not irreducible in the Gaussian integers (prime_iff_mod_four_eq_three_of_nat_prime, from ZMod.exists_sq_eq_neg_one_iff) and applies GaussianInt.sq_add_sq_of_nat_prime_of_not_irreducible; the converse is added here.

statement: Let $w$ be a [word](c:word) with [periods](c:period-of-a-word) $p$ and $q$, where $p, q \ge 1$, and length at least $p + q - \gcd(p, q)$. Then $w$ has period $\gcd(p, q)$. A word has period $p$ when $w_i = w_{i+p}$ for all positions $i$ with $i + p \le |w|$.

hypotheses.text: The word $w$ has [period](c:period-of-a-word) $p \ge 1$.
The word $w$ has [period](c:period-of-a-word) $q \ge 1$.
The length satisfies $|w| \ge p + q - \gcd(p, q)$, with the [greatest common divisor](c:greatest-common-divisor).

formal.difference: mathlib defines a period by $w$ being a prefix of take p w ++ w, and it allows $p$ or $q$ to be $0$, where every word has period $0$. This theorem takes $p, q \ge 1$.

proofs.name: Euclidean induction
proofs.slogan: Subtract the smaller period from the larger one by dropping the first $q$ letters, as in the Euclidean algorithm, and induct on $p + q$.
proofs.scope: For $p, q \ge 1$. If $p = q$ the claim is the hypothesis; otherwise swap to get $p > q$ and write $g = \gcd(p, q)$.

roles.why: Period $p$ shifts letters by $p$, which gives period $p - q$ after the first $q$ letters are dropped.
Period $q$ keeps the dropped word periodic and makes the first $q$ letters repeat in the rest.
The length bound passes to the shorter word with the periods $p - q$ and $q$.

steps.slogan: Drop the first $q$ letters and show that the rest has periods $p - q$ and $q$.
steps.detail: Let $p > q$ and let $w'$ be $w$ without its first $q$ letters. Every factor of $w$ keeps period $q$. Also $w'_{i + p - q} = w_{i+p} = w_i = w_{i+q} = w'_i$, so $w'$ has period $p - q$.

steps.slogan: Check that $w'$ meets the length bound for the pair $(p - q, q)$.
steps.detail: Since $\gcd(p - q, q) = g$, we get $|w'| = |w| - q \ge (p - q) + q - g$. Also $|w'| \ge p - g \ge q$, because $g$ divides $p - q > 0$.

steps.slogan: Apply the claim to $w'$ with the smaller pair of periods.
steps.detail: Since $(p - q) + q < p + q$, the induction hypothesis shows that $w'$ has period $\gcd(p - q, q) = g$.

steps.slogan: Rebuild $w$ from $w'$ and show that $w$ has period $g$.
steps.detail: Write $w = u w'$ with $u$ the first $q$ letters of $w$. As $w$ has period $q$ and $|w'| \ge q$, $u$ is also the first $q$ letters of $w'$. So position $j$ of $w$ holds letter $j$ or $j - q$ of $w'$, equal modulo $g$ since $g \mid q$. Letters of $w'$ at positions equal modulo $g$ agree, so $w$ has period $g$.

concepts.c:word: The theorem is about a finite word and its letters at given positions.
concepts.c:period-of-a-word: A period is the shift that leaves the word unchanged where defined.
concepts.c:greatest-common-divisor: The new period is the gcd, reached by subtracting as in Euclid's algorithm.

source.note: mathlib drops the first q letters (drop_of_hasPeriod_add), inducts on (q, p) with gcd_sub_self_left, and glues with HasPeriod.take_append.

statement: Let $f\colon R \to S$ be a surjective [ring homomorphism](c:ring-homomorphism) of commutative rings. Then $f$ induces a ring isomorphism from the [quotient ring](c:quotient-ring) $R / \ker f$ onto $S$, given by $r + \ker f \mapsto f(r)$.

hypotheses.text: The map $f\colon R \to S$ is a [ring homomorphism](c:ring-homomorphism) of commutative rings.
The map $f$ is [surjective](c:surjection).

conclusion: The map $\bar f\colon R / \ker f \to S$ with $\bar f(r + \ker f) = f(r)$ is a well-defined ring isomorphism.

formal.difference: mathlib allows a noncommutative ring $R$ and a semiring $S$, with the kernel a two-sided ideal. This theorem is the commutative case.

proofs.name: Induced map
proofs.slogan: Define the map on cosets by $f$, check that it is well defined and a ring homomorphism, and show that it is bijective.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, including the zero ring (then $\ker f = R$ and $S = 0$).

roles.why: Preservation of sums and products makes $\bar f$ well defined and a homomorphism, and a trivial kernel makes it injective.
Surjectivity of $f$ gives surjectivity of $\bar f$.

steps.slogan: Show that the map on cosets does not depend on the chosen representative.
steps.detail: The kernel $I = \ker f$ is an [ideal](c:ideal), so the quotient ring $R / I$ exists. If $r + I = r' + I$, then $r - r' \in I$, so $f(r) - f(r') = f(r - r') = 0$.

steps.slogan: Show that the induced map preserves sums, products and the unit.
steps.detail: We have $\bar f((r + I) + (r' + I)) = f(r + r') = f(r) + f(r')$, and the same for products. Also $\bar f(1 + I) = f(1) = 1$. These are the operations of the quotient ring.

steps.slogan: Show that the induced map has trivial kernel and is injective.
steps.detail: If $\bar f(r + I) = f(r) = 0$, then $r \in \ker f = I$, so $r + I = 0$. If $\bar f(a) = \bar f(b)$, then $\bar f(a - b) = 0$, so $a = b$.

steps.slogan: Show that the induced map reaches every element of $S$.
steps.detail: Let $s \in S$. Surjectivity of $f$ gives $r$ with $f(r) = s$, so $\bar f(r + I) = s$.

steps.slogan: Combine bijectivity and the homomorphism property into an isomorphism.
steps.detail: A bijective ring homomorphism has an inverse that is also a ring homomorphism. So $\bar f\colon R / \ker f \to S$ is a ring isomorphism.

concepts.c:ring-homomorphism: The map $f$ respects sums and products, which the induced map inherits.
concepts.c:quotient-ring: The quotient ring is the domain of the induced map.
concepts.c:surjection: Surjectivity of $f$ is what makes the induced map onto $S$.
concepts.c:ideal: The kernel is an ideal, which is what lets us form the quotient ring.

source.note: mathlib builds the forward map by Ideal.Quotient.lift (RingHom.kerLift) and the inverse from a right inverse of f (quotientKerEquivOfRightInverse); here injectivity is checked directly.
